method: Agreement table across ten techniques, followed by a narrative summary

legend.D: dissonant (points the other way or changes with a definition)

conclusions.title: The quotes do not show support for the three hypotheses as a set.
conclusions.text: H1 has a favourable direction from three participants but is not tested as a comparison. H2 and H3 receive no affirming statement, and each is contradicted only by the hypothetical statements of two participants. When 21 changes to the inclusion rules were tried, none produced support for H1 as a comparison, for H2 or for H3.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques agree on the direction. The techniques read the quotes in different ways: the case matrix, hypothesis tree and framework matrix lay the quotes out by participant, the content analysis, stance detection and word-cue count tally them, the thematic analysis reads them for meaning, the competing hypotheses matrix rates them against rival explanations, and the disconfirmation search looked for statements that would overturn the reading and found none. The sensitivity test found no reversal in 21 changed rows. The quotation and spot checks passed. All ten techniques read the same ten quotes and were run by the same model, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and none can see past the material.

conclusions.title: No quote compares the voice AI with traditional voice automation, so H1 as worded is untested.
conclusions.text: The comparators named are website chat bots (P1), a robot voice (P2) and having to repeat yourself (P3). Only P2's remark that a robot "sounds more like a robot voice" refers to a voice system, and it is an indirect comparison. Satisfaction relative to traditional voice automation therefore cannot be read from these quotes.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: Nine techniques agree, and the disconfirmation search partly agrees: it found that P2's remark is one indirect voice comparison, so the wording here says no direct comparison and not no comparison at all. The techniques read the quotes in different ways (tabulation by participant, word-cue counting, stance labels, a search for disconfirming statements, and a re-run with a stricter rule for the comparator). The checks passed. The stance detection repeat run gave the same label on 28 of 30 targets, and the two differences (Q7 on H1, Q10 on H2) do not change which comparators were named. All ten techniques read the same ten quotes and were run by the same model, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and none can see past the material.

conclusions.title: Quoted participants are split on the voice AI, with three favourable and three unfavourable at least once.
conclusions.text: P1, P2 and P3 speak well of it, and P4 reaches approval after initial reluctance. P5 and P10 object, and P1 also records annoyance in a second quote. Depending on how P1, P4 and the context-specific complaints are coded, the split is a tie or four favourable against two unfavourable.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Eight techniques agree on the split, using different readings (participant matrix, tree of sub-claims, themes, stance labels, content codes and a rival-hypotheses rating). The word-cue count only partly agrees because its lexicon wrongly counted the word robot in Q2 as negative. The sensitivity test shows the exact balance changes with the coding. In the stance detection repeat run, the label for Q7 on H1 differed on one of two runs, and Q7 is one of the unfavourable quotes. The label is medium for these reasons, although the checks passed. All ten techniques read the same ten quotes and were run by the same model, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and none can see past the material.

conclusions.title: H2 is untested as worded: no quote links a hang-up to learning that it is an AI.
conclusions.text: P10 says "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro" and gives the reason as "way too long". P5 would probably have hung up only if no human was provided. No quote says a participant would stay on the line, and P4's move from reluctance to approval is at most weak support. The material does not say where the AI is disclosed.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: The techniques agree on the facts but differ in the label they give H2, and the cause is a difference in definition. Where hanging up counts as evidence against H2 whatever its cause (stance detection, word-cue count, framework matrix and the case matrix), H2 is contradicted for two participants. Where the cause must be learning it is an AI, or where hypothetical statements are excluded, H2 is untested (hypothesis tree, thematic analysis, content analysis, and the sensitivity test in rows 8, 12 and 21). This conclusion takes the stricter definition because it is the wording of H2. The stance detection repeat run gave a different label on Q10 for H2 on one of two runs. One verification finding limits it: the disconfirmation search found that P5's reference to "AI in its current state" means the disclosure cannot be ruled out as a driver. All ten techniques read the same ten quotes and were run by the same model, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and none can see past the material.

conclusions.title: H3 is not supported, and two participants say they would ask for a human, as hedged intentions.
conclusions.text: P4 says they would probably want to speak to someone "at first" and, about asking at the introduction, "If I was gonna do it, that's probably where I would do it". P5 says "I would've asked for a human." with no timing. No quote says a participant would decline to ask, and the silence of P1, P2 and P3 is not evidence of a view.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Eight techniques agree that H3 is contradicted for P4 and P5 and that nothing supports it, reading the quotes in different ways (matrix, tree, themes, stance labels, counts and ratings). The disconfirmation search limits the conclusion: P4's statement is hedged twice, the note naming the introduction is the compiler's gloss and not P4's words, and P5 gives no timing, so "immediately" is not confirmed. The sensitivity test shows the contradiction rests on one participant each in several rows and becomes untested when hypothetical statements are excluded. The checks passed. All ten techniques read the same ten quotes and were run by the same model, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and none can see past the material.

conclusions.title: Participants tie reservations to the voice, a stressful setting, a long introduction and earlier experience, but not separably from the AI itself.
conclusions.text: P10 objects that the voice is American and "sounds very much like an AI voice", P5 calls the voice "very cold in clinical" and imagines a car accident, P10 calls the introduction too long, and P1 refers to earlier experiences with AI agents. Several techniques read these as context and not as rejection of voice AI. The disconfirmation search points out that P5 also names "AI in its current state", and that the link between Q7 and the motor claim scenario is inferred, not recorded.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Most techniques agree that reservations point to named features, and they read the quotes in different ways. The conflict is between findings worded as context and not the AI (case matrix, thematic analysis, framework matrix) and the disconfirmation search, which shows that Q4 and Q7 name the AI and that one driver does not cover Q4 and Q6. The cause is the wording of those two quotes combined with the absence of any record of where the AI is disclosed, so the conflict is resolved only by stating several drivers and leaving the AI's own role open, which this conclusion does. A verification finding therefore limits it to medium. All ten techniques read the same ten quotes and were run by the same model, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and none can see past the material.

conclusions.title: Every hang-up and human-request statement is hypothetical, so no behaviour was observed.
conclusions.text: Participants heard prerecorded scenarios, and each relevant statement uses "would" or "if I was". P1's Q6 reports that a human could be requested, which describes what the scenario offered. The quotes therefore show intentions, which may overstate or understate what customers do in a live call.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques agree, using different readings, including a tense check in the disconfirmation search (no observed behaviour found) and a sensitivity row that removes every hypothetical statement. The checks passed. All ten techniques read the same ten quotes and were run by the same model, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and none can see past the material.

conclusions.title: Where leaving or asking for a human is imagined, it is placed at the start of the call.
conclusions.text: P10 places the hang-up "at the intro", and P4's remark about asking for a human is about the introduction. P5 gives no timing, and P4 says the wish to speak to someone changes as the process goes on. The pattern is therefore about the opening moments, and it should not be netted against the favourable reactions, which concern the whole experience.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Three techniques (thematic analysis, framework matrix and content analysis) state the pattern directly, and the others agree in part or list it as an alternative explanation. The wording of the introduction link rests on one explicit quote (Q8) and one quote whose timing comes from the compiler's note (Q9), and the disconfirmation search found that P5 gives no timing. The sensitivity test shows the pattern is not reversed when timing is required, but it then rests on one participant for each behaviour. The checks passed. All ten techniques read the same ten quotes and were run by the same model, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and none can see past the material.

conclusions.title: Two of the eight participants have no quote, and the basis for choosing the quotes is not given.
conclusions.text: P8 and P9 are not quoted, and the material says only that some participants are quoted. Every finding therefore covers six participants and ten selected quotes. If the selection favoured strong reactions, the split between favourable and unfavourable views would be exaggerated.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques report the gap, and the sensitivity test bounded it by assuming invented positions for P8 and P9, which could produce at most a tie. This is a finding about what the material contains, and the checks passed. All ten techniques read the same ten quotes and were run by the same model, so their agreement is not independent evidence, and none can see past the material.

insights.title: The praise for the voice AI is a comparison with worse systems, not with traditional voice automation.
insights.expected: The favourable quotes would show that customers find voice AI more satisfying than the voice automation they know.
insights.found: The favourable comparators are website chat bots, a robot voice and repeating yourself, and no quote names a phone menu or interactive voice response system.
insights.why_it_matters: A favourable reaction in these interviews cannot be used as evidence that voice AI beats the voice automation it would replace.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: C2 is high and C3 is medium, so the insight takes the lower label. The same comparators may also reflect a low baseline from earlier tools, which the quotes cannot separate from real satisfaction.

insights.title: Wanting a human may be a first reaction that fades as the call goes on.
insights.expected: H3 assumes that customers either ask for a human straight away or do not.
insights.found: P4 says they would probably want to speak to someone at first, then finds it "a really good process" as it goes on, so the same participant is on both sides at different points.
insights.why_it_matters: A route to a human at the start may matter more than whether customers keep using it later.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: C5 and C8 are both medium. The fading is stated by one participant in one quote, and no technique had a second participant to compare it with.

insights.title: The stated reasons for hanging up are about the introduction and a refused human, not about learning it is an AI.
insights.expected: H2 assumes that the moment of learning it is an AI is what triggers a hang-up.
insights.found: P10 gives the length of the introduction and P5 makes the hang-up conditional on not getting a human, and the material does not say when the AI is disclosed.
insights.why_it_matters: The contradiction of H2 depends on counting any early exit as evidence, and a design change to the introduction could address both stated reasons.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: C4 and C6 are both medium. The disconfirmation search shows that the AI itself cannot be ruled out as a driver for P5 and P10.

insights.title: The split is within people as well as between them.
insights.expected: The favourable and unfavourable quotes would come from two kinds of customer, enthusiasts and sceptics.
insights.found: P1 is favourable in Q1 and annoyed in Q6, and P4 moves from reluctance to approval in Q5, so the quotes attach to features and moments more than to types of customer.
insights.why_it_matters: Sorting participants into accepting and rejecting groups would misrepresent these interviews.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: C3 and C6 are both medium. The pattern rests on two participants, and the favourable and unfavourable groups may differ in the question each was answering and not in feeling.

paragraphs: Do the eight interviews support the three hypotheses? Not as a set. Of the ten quotes from six participants, the clearest result is that none of the hypotheses is shown in the form it was written, although the evidence leans towards a favourable view of the voice AI for H1 and against H3. Ten techniques, which read the quotes by tabulating, counting, theme reading, stance labelling, rival-hypothesis rating, a search for disconfirming statements and a re-run under changed rules, reached the same overall reading, and no change to the inclusion rules reversed it.

H1 is partly supported in direction. P1, P2 and P3 speak well of the AI and P4 comes round to it, while P5 and P10 object and P1 is annoyed in a second quote, so the quoted participants are split. No quote compares the AI with traditional voice automation. The comparators are chat bots, a robot voice and having to repeat yourself, so the hypothesis cannot be tested as written, and the praise is better read as relief from worse experiences. The split is a tie or four against two depending on coding, and one repeat run of the stance detection gave a different label for Q7, so the balance is medium confidence.

H2 and H3 are where the techniques disagreed on the label and agreed on the facts. P10 would have hung up at the intro and P5 would probably have hung up if no human was offered. P4 would probably ask for a human at the introduction and P5 would ask. If any early exit or request counts, H2 and H3 are contradicted for two participants each. If the cause of the hang-up must be learning it is an AI, or if hypothetical statements are excluded, both become untested. The cause of the conflict is therefore the definition used, not a difference in what the participants said. H2 and H3 are both medium confidence because P4's statement is hedged, P5 gives no timing and the material does not say where the AI is disclosed.

The reasons participants give are specific: the American voice, a cold voice, a stressful car accident, a long introduction and earlier experience with AI agents. These point to context and delivery more than to rejection of voice AI, but the disconfirmation search shows that P5 and P10 also name the AI, and the link between Q7 and the motor claim scenario is inferred. Whether the AI itself, as distinct from these features, drives the reactions is unresolved. Where leaving or asking is imagined, it is at the start of the call, and P4's wish for a human fades.

For the decision, the findings describe six participants and ten selected quotes. P8 and P9 have no quote, the basis for choosing the quotes is unknown, and every hang-up and human-request statement is hypothetical, from people who heard prerecorded scenarios. All techniques read the same material and were run by the same model, so their agreement is a check on method and not independent evidence. The quotation and spot checks passed, and no person reviewed the results. The findings show a link between a human-sounding voice and approval, and between the opening of the call and the wish to leave or reach a person, and they cannot show how common either pattern is.
